# Week 4, Day 2.1 — Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Both of today's topics are locator work plus an options object.

| You'll use | Taught in |
|---|---|
| Locators and chaining | [week3/day3_2](/learn/w3/d3/p2) |
| Options objects (`{ button: "right" }`) | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| `async` / `await` | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| Reading an error message | [day1_2](/learn/w4/d1/p2) |

That last row matters more than usual: half of today is telling two error messages apart.

One new **shape** worth naming before you meet it — listening for a browser dialog:

```ts
page.once("dialog", async (dialog) => { await dialog.accept(); });
```

`page.once` registers a callback that fires at most once. Set it up **before** the action that
triggers the dialog; by the time the dialog exists it's too late to start listening.

**Next:** [Day 2.2 — Elements you can't reach](/learn/w4/d2/p2)

# Week 4, Day 2.2 — Elements you can't reach

Two different ways a correct locator fails you. Sometimes the element is behind a boundary your
locator can't cross. Sometimes it only exists while you're pointing at it.

By the end of this lesson you can handle both, and tell them apart in seconds.

> **Mode: explore.** Write code in the editor and press Run — it drives a real browser and shows you what happened.

## Part 1 — Frames

An `<iframe>` is a whole second document embedded in the page. It has its own DOM, and the outer
page's locators **cannot see into it**.

The mall analogy is a good one: the dress is behind glass. You can see it perfectly, point at it,
describe it — and still can't pick it up until you open the case.

| Tool | How you cross the boundary |
|---|---|
| Selenium | `driver.switchTo().frame(...)`, then switch back |
| Playwright | `page.frameLocator(...)` — no switching, no state to restore |

Playwright's version has no "current frame" to forget about, which removes a whole class of bug
where a later locator silently searches the wrong document.
## Example 1 — the failure, on purpose

**Expected:**

```
iframes on the page:  1
#tinymce from page:   0
iframe id attribute:  mce_0_ifr
```

**Zero.** The element is visible in a real browser, your selector is correct, and the page reports it
does not exist. This is the wall students hit for twenty minutes.

The tell is that first line: **there is an iframe on the page.** Whenever a locator you trust returns
0, check for frames before doubting the locator.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
## Example 2 — crossing the boundary

**Expected:** `1`, then `"Your content goes here."`

`frameLocator("#mce_0_ifr")` says *"find that iframe, then look inside it"*. Read it as a path:
**page → frame → element.** Miss the middle step and you get zero.

**Challenge:** try `page.frameLocator("#does-not-exist").locator("body").count()`. What happens, and
how long does it take?

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 3 — two failures that look alike

The diagnostic skill that saves the twenty minutes.

**Expected:** roughly

```
no frameLocator -> 2011ms | locator.click: Timeout 2000ms exceeded.
with frameLocator -> 46ms | locator.fill: Error: Element is not an <input>, <textarea>, ...
```

Two things separate them, and both are diagnostic:

| | Time | Message |
|---|---|---|
| Never found it | spends the **whole deadline** | `Timeout … exceeded` |
| Found it, refused the action | fails **immediately** | describes the element |

**A fast failure means Playwright found your element.** So the locator is fine and the problem is the
element — read-only here, or disabled, or covered. A slow failure means it never matched, and *that's*
when to suspect a frame.

(This editor happens to be read-only, which gives us the second failure mode for free.)

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
## Example 4 — frames inside frames

**Expected:** `"MIDDLE"`, `"BOTTOM"`, then `0`.

That last line is the point. `frame-bottom` is not inside `frame-top`, so chaining through it finds
nothing — and you get a *timeout*, sending you after the wrong problem.

**Match the chain to the nesting.** Open the DOM, find the frame that actually contains your element,
and count the boundaries between it and the page.

> **Finding the frame:** `Ctrl+F` the DOM for `frame`, click through the hits until the highlight
> covers your element's region, then read its `name` or `id`. And `npx playwright codegen` records
> frame boundaries for you automatically — the session deliberately told students *not* to record the
> exercise, because recording would have solved it instantly and taught them nothing about the failure.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Part 2 — Gestures

The other way a correct locator isn't enough: the element only appears while the pointer is over it,
or only reacts to a right-click.

In Selenium each of these needed an `Actions` builder and three lines. Playwright folded the family
into the locator:

| Selenium `Actions` | Playwright |
|---|---|
| `moveToElement(e).perform()` | `locator.hover()` |
| `contextClick(e).perform()` | `locator.click({ button: "right" })` |
| `doubleClick(e).perform()` | `locator.dblclick()` |
| `dragAndDrop(a, b).perform()` | `a.dragTo(b)` |

Same capability, one line, and it auto-waits for the element to be ready.
## Example 5 — hover

**Expected:** `3`, `false`, `true`, `"name: user1 View profile"`.

One call. No builder, no `.perform()`, and `hover()` waits for the element to be visible and stable
first.

**The trap:** the caption is in the DOM the whole time — only its CSS changes. So `toBeVisible()` is
the right assertion and `count()` is the wrong one. `count()` returns 1 either way, and a test built
on it passes **without hovering at all**.

Both forms work — `page.hover(sel)` and `page.locator(sel).hover()` — but prefer the locator form: it
composes with `.first()`, `.nth()`, `.filter()`, and reads like the rest of your suite.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
## Example 6 — right-click, and the click options

**Expected:** `dialog said: "You selected a context menu"`, then the confirmation line.

**`{ button: "right" }`, not a new method.** Same for `"middle"`.

**The listener goes first.** A JS dialog blocks the page until something dismisses it. Attach the
handler after the click and the test hangs until it times out — a confusing failure, because the code
looks right.

| Option | For |
|---|---|
| `button` | `"left"` / `"right"` / `"middle"` |
| `clickCount` | 2 is a double-click; `dblclick()` says it better |
| `delay` | widgets that measure how long you held the button |
| `position` | canvases, image maps, sliders |
| `force` | skips the actionability checks — **a warning sign**, not a tool |

`force: true` turns "this element isn't clickable" into "clicked something invisible and moved on".
If you need it, the interesting question is why the element isn't ready.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
## Example 7 — drag and drop

**Expected:** `A` before, `B` after — the columns swap contents.

`dragTo()` replaces the whole Selenium dance. When it doesn't work — some custom widgets listen for
raw pointer events rather than HTML5 drag — the manual route is `hover()` → `mouse.down()` → hover the
target → `mouse.up()`. Reach for that only after `dragTo` has failed.

**Assert on the consequence, not the gesture.** The header text changing proves the drop registered.
"No error was thrown" does not.
## Both halves, as real specs

> ▶ **Run them yourself:**
> ```
> npx playwright test week4/generated/day2-frames.spec.ts
> npx playwright test week4/generated/day2-mouse-actions.spec.ts
> ```

**Expected:** `6 passed` and `5 passed`.

The frames spec asserts the **failures** as well as the successes — `toHaveCount(0)` without a frame
locator, and the two distinguishable error messages. A test documenting how something fails is as
useful as one documenting how it works, and it stays green.

The mouse spec swaps two explore-cell shortcuts for their spec equivalents: `toBeHidden()` instead of
`isVisible()` (it auto-waits, so it can't read the state a millisecond too early), and
`expect.poll(() => message)` instead of `waitForTimeout` — waiting for the **condition** rather than
guessing at 500 ms.

## Best practices

- **Locator returns 0 and you trust it?** Count the iframes before touching the selector.
- **One `frameLocator` per boundary**, matching the real nesting.
- **Register dialog handlers before the action** that triggers them.
- **Assert the consequence** of a gesture, not that it didn't throw.
- **Treat `force: true` as a question**, not a fix.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Count 0 on a visible element | it's inside a frame | `page.frameLocator(...)` first |
| Timeout chaining nested frames | wrong hierarchy | check which frame really contains it |
| `Element is not an <input>` | you're in the right place | it's read-only/disabled, not missing |
| Test hangs after a right-click | no dialog handler, or too late | `page.once("dialog", …)` before the click |
| Hover test passes without hovering | asserted on `count()` | `toBeVisible()` / `toBeHidden()` |
| `dragTo` does nothing | widget uses raw pointer events | manual `mouse.down()` / `mouse.up()` |

**Next:** [Day 2.3](/learn/w4/d2/p3) — hiding both behind a page object.

# Week 4, Day 2.3 — Hiding the mechanics

Same API as [Day 2.2](/learn/w4/d2/p2). No new calls. The question is who should know that a frame or a
hover menu is involved — and the answer for both is *not the test*.

## Both are implementation details

A frame is a decision the **developers** made about page structure. A hover menu is a decision the
**designers** made about interaction. Your test is about what a *user achieved*.

So both of these have leaked someone else's choice into the test:

```ts
await page.frameLocator("#mce_0_ifr").locator("body").click();
await page.locator("#nav-account").hover();
await page.locator("#nav-account .dropdown >> text=Sign out").click();
```

| In the test | Behind a class |
|---|---|
| `frameLocator("#mce_0_ifr").locator("body")` | `editor.body` |
| `hover()` then `waitFor()` then `click()` | `await nav.signOut()` |
| breaks when the frame id or menu style changes | one field or method changes |

When iframes go out of fashion, or the menu becomes click-to-open, the wrapped version is a one-line
change and no test notices.

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| `frameLocator` in the constructor | one place knows about the boundary |
| `frame` and `trigger` are `private` | no test can reach past the abstraction |
| `body` / `caption()` return plain `Locator`s | callers can't tell a frame or hover was involved |
| Selectors are **constructor parameters** | one class serves every frame / every menu on the site |
| `open()` waits for the panel | `hover()` returning ≠ the menu opened; CSS transitions take time |
| No `expect()` anywhere | same rule as [week3/day3_3](/learn/w3/d3/p3) |

`FrameLocator` is worth naming as a type: it isn't a `Locator` and has no `.click()` of its own. It's
a **doorway** — you chain a locator off it.

That "`open()` waits" row is the one that saves you. Waiting inside `open()` means every caller gets
it right without knowing they needed to.

## Where each thing belongs

| Action | Page object or test? |
|---|---|
| crossing a frame boundary | **page object** — it's page structure |
| `hover()` to open a menu | **page object** — it's how the menu works |
| `dragTo()` to reorder a list | **page object** — `reorder(from, to)` |
| `click({ button: "right" })` for a context menu | **page object** — `openContextMenu(row)` |
| asserting the menu opened | **test** |
| asserting the list order changed | **test** |

One line covers both halves of today: **gestures and boundaries are mechanics; outcomes are
assertions.**

### Where frames genuinely leak

Some things a page object can't hide, and it's better to know which:

| Situation | Why it leaks |
|---|---|
| Payment iframes (Stripe, PayPal) | third-party markup you don't control |
| A frame that appears only sometimes | the caller must handle both shapes |
| Cross-origin frames | some APIs behave differently |

For third-party payment frames the honest advice is **don't test through them at all** where you can
avoid it: stub the provider at the network layer and test your own pages. Driving a vendor's iframe
couples your suite to their release schedule.

## What a reviewer checks

- **No `frameLocator` or bare `hover()` in a test** — both belong behind a named method.
- **Selectors passed in**, not hardcoded in the class.
- **The open method waits** for what the gesture reveals.
- **No `expect()`** inside the class.
- **Third-party frames questioned** — is there a stub instead?

**Next:** [Day 2.4](/learn/w4/d2/p4) — your turn.

# Week 4, Day 2.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

Verified targets, all on `the-internet.herokuapp.com`:

| Page | Facts |
|---|---|
| `/iframe` | 1 iframe, `id="mce_0_ifr"`; body text `"Your content goes here."`; **read-only** |
| `/nested_frames` | `frame-top` → `frame-left`/`frame-middle`/`frame-right`; `frame-bottom` is a **sibling** |
| `/hovers` | 3 × `.figure`; `.figcaption` hidden until hover; `"name: user1 View profile"` |
| `/context_menu` | `#hot-spot`; right-click fires a dialog `"You selected a context menu"` |
| `/drag_and_drop` | `#column-a` / `#column-b`; headers swap `A` → `B` |

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 2.2](/learn/w4/d2/p2).

## When you're done

**Count the `frameLocator` and `hover()` calls visible in your Problem 3 spec.** Zero is the target. A
test should describe what a person read and did; whether the developers used an iframe, or the
designers used a hover menu, is not the test's business.

**Next:** [Day 3.1](/learn/w4/d3/p1) — changing settings without disturbing your team.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Document a frame failure before fixing it, and a hover that can't cheat.

**Part A** — on `/iframe`: assert `#tinymce` has count **0** from the page, assert there **is** one
iframe, then assert count **1** through `frameLocator`, then assert its text.

**Part B** — on `/hovers`: for each of the 3 figures, assert the caption is hidden, hover, assert
visible, and assert each names a different user. Use a loop, not three copy-pasted blocks.

**Check yourself.** All pass. Then **delete the `hover()` calls** and confirm Part B now fails — if it
still passes, you asserted on the wrong thing and never tested hovering at all.

> **Hint** — that deletion check is the real exercise. `count()` and `toBeVisible()` behave very
> differently here.

**Build.** Reach all four nested frames, and assert both consequences of a drag.

1. On `/nested_frames`, assert the text of **left**, **middle**, **right** and **bottom**. Three live
   inside `frame-top`; one does not.
2. On `/drag_and_drop`, drag A onto B and assert **both** headers — then drag back and assert the
   original order returns.
3. On `/context_menu`, right-click and assert the dialog message **exactly**; then dismiss with
   `dialog.dismiss()` instead of `accept()` and note any difference.

**Where.** A spec in `week4/generated/`.

**Check yourself.** All pass. Then deliberately chain `frame-bottom` through `frame-top` and record
how long the failure takes and what it says — that timing is the diagnostic from Day 2.2. Also remove
the dialog handler and watch what happens.

> **Hint** — step 2's "drag back" is a fair check on step 2. If the order doesn't restore, one of your
> assertions measured the wrong element.

**Build.** Two classes that hide every boundary and every gesture.

1. A `NestedFramesPage` taking a `Page`, with `left`, `middle`, `right`, `bottom` each returning a
   `Locator` — frame names supplied to the **constructor**
2. A `HoverMenu` taking a `Page` and a trigger selector, with `open()` (hovers **and waits**),
   `caption()`, and `choose(text)`
3. A spec using both, with **no `frameLocator` and no bare `hover()` anywhere in the spec**

**Where.** Helper `.ts` files plus a spec in `week4/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `frameLocator` or `hover()` in the spec file**
- **No `expect()` in either class**
- **No `waitForTimeout`**
- Every test passes **run on its own**

Then make two changes and confirm no test needs editing: point `HoverMenu` at a **click**-to-open
menu (swap `hover()` for `click()` in the class), and point `NestedFramesPage` at `/iframe` with a
different frame selector.

**Check yourself.** Passes together, alone, and with `--workers=4`. Both swaps require touching only
the classes.

> **Hint** — if you had to edit a single test for either swap, something leaked out of the class. That
> is the whole exercise.
